utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Judge Nosworthy is still unwell. We shall continue in her absence on the same basis as yesterday and we shall continue with the cross-examination of Mr. Vojnovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The cross-examination by Mr. Hannis will continue in a moment. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you gave at the beginning of your evidence, that continues to apply to that evidence today. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Vojnovic. I realized there were two additional questions I wanted to ask you about your written statement, Exhibit 6D1532, and the first one relates to paragraph 38. In that you mentioned refugee convoys were often bombed and you said: "I was in one such convoy where many people were killed as a result." What convoy were you in? You were in a refugee convoy?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I was returning from Djakovica going to Prizren on that day, around 2.00 p.m. There were many people on the road, vehicles, tractors, et cetera. Some 300 metres in front of me a tractor was hit by a shell. There were some 30 people there including women and children. There was -- the road between Djakovica and Prizren is some 60 kilometres long. There were other columns and there were more strikes, but that was the one I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how were you travelling? You weren't in the convoy then; that's not a correct statement, right? You just saw it from a distance of about 300 metres?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't one single long column. There were several groups of people moving from Prizren to Djakovica, that is, they were going back. I was in a vehicle and I saw it from the vehicle. I was trying to get away as soon as possible as well. I wasn't alone. There were two policemen with me or maybe the driver and one or two other policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what kind of vehicle were you in? Were you in a police vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was the property of the police, but I think it was a black civilian car, I think it was an Audi.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the second thing I wanted to ask you about in your statement, Exhibit -- at paragraph 34 you say how the police took all measures to protect lives and property and you didn't tolerate any illegal behaviour regardless of ethnicity or position. And then there's a reference to Exhibit 6D365 I guess as an example of this, and I would like to show you Exhibit 6D365 and ask you a couple of questions about it. I can hand you a hard copy because it's several pages, and this appears to be at least in part a part of a criminal report regarding Vukajlo Vulic. The first page is dated the 30th of March, 1999. Do you see that? Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Hannis, please

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember the case that this refers to?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you go to page 8 of the English for Your Honours and we English speakers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's page 5 of your document, sir, and it talks about reasonable suspicion against Mr. Vulic and another individual as well as the third accused Nebojsa Lalic and the fourth accused Zoran Radovic. Those last two are described as policemen from the Prizren police station, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And from my reading of this document, I gather the essence of this event was there were a couple of Albanian families who were trying to leave Kosovo, they engaged the assistance of two non-policemen, who then engaged the assistance of Mr. Lalic and Mr. Radovic, the policemen, to help those Albanian families get out of Kosovo, right? Is that a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the essence is that they wanted money for that favour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Right. And if you would go to page 9 in your copy, and in the English it's the 14th page of this exhibit, and this is dated the 4th of April, 1999, and it's a report regarding a severe violation of official duties against Nebojsa Lalic. I note in the first paragraph there it indicates that he had been with the MUP since June of 1992, he was a sergeant first class, and that he had been sanctioned in the past. Do you know what the previous sanction was for, Mr. Vojnovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Toward the -- the third paragraph under that report, it's apparently a finding that he committed the following severe violations of official duties, and it included behaviour damaging the reputation of the service and illegal obtaining of personal or material gain. And if we could scroll to the bottom of the B/C/S page and if we could go to the next page in the English on the e-court, we'll see the writer of this report is proposing that policeman Lalic be fined on a disciplinary measure amounting to 20 per cent of his salary over a three-month period and: "I propose the disciplinary measuring of lowering of rank for a two-year period." Now, you told us about your work on the MUP disciplinary court. Is this -- is there any other sentence being recommended here? No loss of job, no jail time, nothing like that, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not right. If I may, I'll explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a report of a grave breach of official duty drafted on the basis of the decree on internal affairs as the lex specialis current legislation at the time. In addition to this, there was another report submitted to the prosecutor's office against the same perpetrators, whereby they could also receive a prison sentence. If there is an order to conduct an investigation, according to the Law on Working Relations, they -- their employment is terminated. This report was written under one particular law, whereas the crime, the act, they committed is also regulated by another piece of legislation; however, that did not fall under my authority or the authority of the disciplinary court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But we see no reference in this document relating to event about a referral to any other court, do we? At least I didn't read anything in my English version.

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we cannot see that. This report was drafted by his commander. The criminal report was drafted by the inspector who investigated the incident. We don't know whether a separate investigation was initiated which could result in a separate request for their employment to be terminated, and of course it should be followed by a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, in introducing this passage of evidence you described this document as part of a criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What in fact is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The first page is listed as a criminal report, the first page of this exhibit, and this page that I've been reading from now is a separate document dated the 4th of April and it's described as a report in accordance with paragraph 3, Article 9 of the decree on internal affairs in a state of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So do we get assistance on whether there were criminal proceedings in the first part?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I don't see it anywhere in this exhibit number 6D365.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, this event involved an amount of money of about 10.000 German marks was the bribe that was being offered by these Albanian families who wanted to leave. At that time, in 1999, can you tell us about how many dinars that was in Kosovo, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall, I can't speculate. I cannot tell you offhand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me try it another way. My sense is it's a fairly large sum of money. How much would a sergeant first class in the MUP make in a year in 1999 in Kosovo, any idea?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot of time has passed. 10.000 was probably the cost of a new car, maybe the Zastava 101 car or more. I cannot recall at this moment what my salary was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, that was my next question. You don't remember how much you got paid as chief of the SUP in Prizren in 1999, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to think about it. Well, maybe around 200 German marks more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that per month or per year?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Per month.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. There's nothing in this exhibit either that refers to what happened to the second policeman involved in this, Zoran Radovic. Do you know whether he was disciplined or had any civil criminal proceedings brought against him?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly don't know. I cannot recall whether they were both from the police station in Prizren. Maybe he was working in another police station and the cases may have been treated separately, although I truly cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I would tell you that at page 5 of the B/C/S and page 8 of the English it indicates that Zoran Radovic also was a policeman from the Prizren police station. The writer of this report, the last page of the document, is -- I can't read the name, it's Lieutenant Milos, it looks like Skekic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Scekic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, even if I could read that, I wouldn't have been able to pronounce it. Tell me, what's the difference or what's the relationship between the Prizren police station and the Prizren SUP that you were the head of?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The secretariat in Prizren had the authority and duty to perform the tasks and authorities from the authority of the MUP in the entire area of Prizren, which encompasses four municipalities: Orahovac, Suva Reka, Prizren, and Dragas. The seat of the secretariat of internal affairs of Prizren was in Prizren itself. As for the other municipalities, Dragas, Orahovac, and Suva Reka, there were separate units or the so-called territorial units and we called OUPs, departments of internal affairs, and they were the ones in charge of MUP tasks in their respective areas. In the seat of the secretariat there are internal organizational units such as the crime police department, et cetera, and within one of those there is the police station --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there. Is that then what we have heard referred to as the OUP, the O-U-P, as opposed to the SUP?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, O-U-P.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm clear. And what was the relationship between you and the commander of the police station, did he report to you? Did he work for you? What was the relationship between you two?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was about to complete my answer to make it clear. The police station in Prizren fell under the police department in Prizren. The police department is one of the internal organizational units of the secretariat of internal affairs. That police station was at the level of an OUP and it was comprised of uniformed policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask you about something that I don't know if you know about or not. In the notice, the Rule 65 ter notice we got from the Defence lawyers advising us that you were going to be a witness and what you were going to testify about, it mentioned that you might speak about Crisis Staff in Prizren, but I don't recall you speaking of that when you testified in direct. Was there a Crisis Staff in Prizren in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the municipal president kept insisting at the beginning of the war, a Crisis Staff was formed in the municipality. I was a member of the staff. After we met -- once when we actually established the staff we never met again, there were no conditions in place for that. Some people referred to it as Crisis Staff, but I believe it should have been called an All People's Defence Staff under the Law on Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did you meet the one time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the bombing started, when the state of war was declared.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Prior to the start of the bombing and after your arrival in January 1999, were you as the chief of the SUP involved in any defence planning for the defence of the populated area of Prizren?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have any dealings with the civil protection staff or the civil defence people?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially were there no dealings, but we met on occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You weren't aware of instructions from July 1998 issued by the Joint Command for the defence of populated areas, were you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The civil defence people, what kind of uniforms did they wear?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I'm not well-acquainted with military terminology. I keep mixing civil defence and civil protection. I know that civil defence had blue suits, like overalls. As for civilian defence, they had grey suits or uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In both those answers you were translated as having referred to civil defence, but you said one had blue suits like overalls and one had grey suits. Which did the civil protection wear, the blue or the grey?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I meant to say civilian protection, the blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And civil defence wore the grey?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me it seems the same from this place. I cannot distinguish between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me then go to a few of the documents remaining that I needed to ask you about. When we finished yesterday we had been looking at P1996. I think I had one or two more questions for you about that document, and this is from the meeting at the MUP staff for Kosovo in Pristina on the 7th of May, 1999. I can hand you the hard copy, that may help. Thank you. We spoke yesterday about the part of the meeting where you spoke and mentioned speaking with the judges in your community, and if you could turn to page 9 of the B/C/S, that's page 10 of the English. And I will tell you that General Lukic is speaking. I think you were asked about this. He mentioned that the number of 27 crimes of murder is not realistic. You explained some possible reasons for that discrepancy, and if you'll go down to the I think it's the fourth bullet point General Lukic is saying: "You must not wait in cases of arson and murder; the suspect must be handed over together with the criminal report to the competent judge at once ..." And then he goes on to say: "These sorts of problems have still not been cleared up ..." and he names some municipalities, including Prizren. What kind of problems had you had in Prizren with not turning suspects and criminal reports over to the competent judges at once, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall at this moment, this was stressed as far as I understood because the courts were being inactive, or rather, they would simply release the suspects the same day, the judges there would. There were no cases of arson in Prizren. I told you that during the war only one house burned down. Whether General Lukic had other information from the daily reports we sent to the MUP and the staff, I don't know, but I cannot tell you precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't look like General Lukic is complaining about the judges; he's complaining that the cases aren't being turned over right away. You don't recall any problems -- since you say there was only one arson, you don't recall any problems with murder cases where the suspects and the criminal reports were not being turned over promptly in Prizren in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any such cases. As a rule a person being handed over to a judge has to have a criminal report filed against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, was that the nature of the problem then, the criminal reports were not being prepared quickly enough?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understand the item above this, that a small number of 27 crimes happened, I think this is lack of expeditiousness because more inspections, on-site investigations were carried out than criminal reports filed. So then the records did not tally, and of course there was no time to compile a record and obtain all the other documentation needed in the file on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me have you go to the last page of this meeting on the 7th of May. I think you touched on this topic before. I think it's the fourth bullet point up from the bottom of the page in your B/C/S, and General -- I think this is General Lukic speaking as well, says: "I especially mention that in the work of the OPG, the chief of SUP gives his permission for certain actions and informs the head of staff about them." Now, you were asked on direct examination by Mr. Lukic about your understanding of this, and you answered a question about: Did the staff command and use OPGs, and you said no. But as the chief of SUP in Prizren, did you have an OPG or more than one OPG in Prizren in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I take it that sometime during 1999 before leaving in June, they took part in some activities or actions against the terrorists, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They helped me in the carrying out of regular tasks and duties of greater complexity than usual. For example, dealing with perpetrators of aggravated crimes. They laid ambushes, they went to provide security where needed and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did they not participate in any anti-terrorist actions?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did, as part of the PJP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And some of those included the joint actions with the army?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, they were part of the PJP company and they went where their company went. They were not the OPG then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And by that you are referring to the 5th Company, the 5th PJP Company from Prizren?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you give permission for their involvement in those actions?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were part of the PJP with the others. They didn't need anyone's approval, or rather, they didn't need mine or my permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So in 1999 did your OPG ever take part in any actions other than as part of the 5th PJP Company? Did they ever take part in an action where they were operating solely as an OPG?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the carrying out of regular tasks and assignments. I've already mentioned that. For example, if we had information that a person of security-related interest was to pass along a certain passage or a certain route or if a person for whom an arrest warrant had been issued was expected to come along because he was a criminal, then part of that OPG was engaged or the entire OPG, but usually it was just part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for those actions did you as SUP chief give your permission?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you inform General Lukic of those actions?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, these were regular tasks and assignments. These tasks and assignments, when it was assessed that there was no security risk for the people, they would be carried by one or more patrols. So between the patrols and the members of the OPG, the only difference was that the members of the OPG were younger men and better trained.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, if I could have you then go back to page 9 of this document, and it's page 11 of the English, that leaves one question still unanswered in my mind. From the bottom of the page, if you'll go up -- there are two lines, the next paragraph, and the paragraph above that. Can you find a part that reads: "In the organization of work" -- and this is on page 11 of the English near the middle. "In the organization of work, the secretariat of the interior must ensure that in Kosovo and Metohija the organization is such that all OPJPs are subordinated to the chief of the secretariat." And this is General Stevanovic speaking, by the way. But from what you've told us before, that doesn't sound like that's what happened in Prizren at any rate. Were the OPJPs subordinated to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Never during 1999 through the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only when there was a joint daily roster did they carry out regular tasks and assignments with the regular policemen of the SUP, and even then it was a PJP officer who was in charge of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So why wasn't this statement from General Stevanovic followed or complied with? Was there some later change in that statement or did you just ignore it? Why wasn't it done?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be precise now, but in the manner of describing -- of carrying out tasks and assignments that I described, there were no problems in practice, everybody did their job in compliance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, that takes me to a point that I've put to some other witnesses regarding the issue of subordination of the MUP to the VJ. You're aware that there was an order issued along the military lines about the MUP being subordinated to the VJ for purposes of combat activities. You knew about that, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw that, but I heard about that story.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we've heard evidence that it never actually got implemented on the MUP side, but it really wasn't a problem on the ground, was it, because you had good coordination between the MUP, the police, and the army, at least in Prizren you had good cooperation with the army in those joint activities against the terrorists, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In this document in the last paragraph there is a discussion about wearing the police uniform and that the green uniform can only be worn in anti-terrorist actions. You told us that you personally did not wear a uniform. Who else in the SUP did not wear a uniform? Were you the only one as the chief?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the rules on the internal organization and the job descriptions within the ministry, inter alia people with P status wore uniforms; people with OSL status did not wear uniforms; people with OD status did not wear uniforms, and nobody else wore uniforms. So to clarify. All those whose status was P, P, police, they wore a uniform -- well, it used to be M, milicija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Right. And the next-to-the-last point in this document was that members of the reserve police station may not wear police uniforms, and this must be prohibited immediately. This is from the meeting of 7 May. To me that sounds like before the 7th of May there was a problem with reserve police wearing police uniforms; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the reserve force could wear uniforms only when they were on the job; however, as I've already said on one occasion, there were isolated cases of lack of discipline when individuals wore uniforms when they were not on the job, and of course this was not permitted. That's why this was highlighted here, to enforce discipline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, you referred to people with OSL status and people with OD status not wearing uniforms. What do these expressions mean, OSL and OD?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] OSL is authorised official persons, these were in fact inspectors of the crime detection department, and there were of course people with the same status in other departments but far fewer. OD means certain duties, and they had the same status as the OSL but not the same powers, not the same authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what do you mean by "certain duties"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for example, they work by day and by night, in shifts, on Sundays, on workdays, but they are not authorised to arrest people, to inspect people's identity papers, to bring people in, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean they are not full policemen, they have some auxiliary status?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards policemen -- well, they weren't even auxiliary policemen. They couldn't inspect people's identity papers or bring people in. They worked as analysts, for example, and gave information to policemen. They had to work by day and by night and in shifts because the analysis department where they had data, for example, on people's criminal records, they couldn't shut down on Sundays, they had to work around-the-clock. So to motivate these people, they were given this status, OD, or certain duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Vojnovic, I need to qualify that answer. You say they couldn't do these things, they couldn't inspect people's identity papers or bring people in, but I would suggest to you that if they're wearing the uniform and they have a gun, they could do it even though they weren't allowed to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, these are people the witness said did not wear uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I thought he was referring to some of the reserve policemen who were wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That was a separate matter I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me move on to a question you were asked yesterday by Mr. Lukic. He asked you if you knew that around the 31st of March, 1999, some -- here it's translated as 80 per cent but I think he was reading from the indictment which is 80.000 Kosovar Albanians gathered in the municipality of Suva Reka at Belanica, and the next day forces of Serbia and Yugoslavia shelled the village and forced the displaced persons to flee. You said you didn't have such information at your disposal. Did you never hear about several thousand Kosovar Albanian civilians in the vicinity of Belanica at the end of March 1999? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards Belanica, I don't know and I didn't know where that village is, but on the main roads from the direction of Suva Reka or Pristina in the direction of Prizren and from Djakovica via Orahovac towards Prizren and then on towards the Albanian border there were many thousands of refugees. I saw that myself. It wasn't impossible to see, but that they were shelled by members of the army and the police, that's something I really don't know and I didn't know that then either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you an exhibit, this is Exhibit Number P2002. I'll hand you a hard copy. This is one you again may not have seen, it's an analysis or report post-action from Colonel Delic of the 549th about actions to destroy the Siptar terrorists in the general area of Malisevo and Pagarusa in the period from 30 March to 3 April 1999. Now, if you could go to page 2 in the B/C/S -- well -- yeah, I think I asked you the other day about the involvement of the 5th PJP Company and the 37th PJP Detachment. On page 2 in your B/C/S and page 3 of the English, if you can find the portion for me right above the paragraph that says: "During the second day of combat operations ..." Do you find that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of the first day?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, during the second day. Do you find that reference?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Two paragraphs above that there's a reference to battle group 5 of the 549th Motorised Brigade and the 37th PJP Detachment had completely seized Dobrodeljane village and two lines below that there's a reference to battle group 2 of the 243rd Motorised Brigade with a company of the 37th PJP having completely seized Semetiste village. Were you aware of those accomplishments of the 37th PJP Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report for the period from the 30th of March to the 3rd of April. Anti-terrorist activities were started by members of the army and the MUP to the best of my recollection on the 25th. In the area between Prizren, Orahovac, and Suva Reka, according to the assessment at the time there was several thousand Siptar terrorists there, and of course I knew that they had passed through that area and that practically it was the territorial detachment of the PJP, this one, that remained behind, but I really cannot recall anything about these particular villages. I'm speaking about the entire territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me have you then go on. Can you find the section that starts with: "During the third day of combat operations the remaining areas were mopped up, the 23rd PJP Detachment and battle group 6 of the 549th ..." Do you find that? I think it's about five paragraphs up from the bottom of that page.

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the second half of that paragraph you see the part that says: "Parts of the 15th Armoured Brigade took Kravasarija village, battle group 2 of the 243rd seized the Kostrce feature and Mahala in the general area of that village," and then "the forces of the 5th PJP company and parts of the 15th Armoured Brigade were joined in Belanica village, where they evacuated and cared for some 30.000 refugees." How do you know about how the 5th PJP Company participated in evacuating some 30.000 refugees? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this particular case. The PJP was usually not involved in these tasks. Problems of providing security for the refugees was something that regular policemen dealt with. Where the refugees were coming from, I really don't know, but I can tell you that there was several thousand on the roads I've already mentioned. Whether they came from the Prizren area or some other areas I can't say because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, we've had some witnesses tell us that they were evacuated by being directed to leave Kosovo and go to Albania. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who sent them there. I myself had an opportunity to speak to those people in those convoys, and of course I tried to persuade them to go back and there are instances where they did but most of them didn't. When I asked them, of course I was wearing civilian clothes and they didn't know I was the chief of the SUP, I asked them where they were going and why; and usually they said they were afraid of the air-strikes --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're not answering my question anymore, so let me move on to another one. When did you first become aware that Colonel Mitrovic had been arrested in connection with the killings of the Berisha family in Suva Reka? When did you first find out about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was still working, it might have been in 2005 or 2004, but just after he was arrested I heard about it because I was working in the MUP and I heard that from a colleague of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And prior to that date had you not heard anything about the killing of a few dozen members of the Berisha family in Suva Reka in late March 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I understand you say you didn't have that information. My question was: Did you not hear about it? You never heard anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you first heard about it in -- I guess it would have been 2005 or 2004 when Mitrovic was arrested, did you make any inquiries to try and find out what that was about because that was a pretty serious crime that happened in your area of responsibility while you were SUP chief? Did you do any checking?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was interviewed about those circumstances and I made a statement before the court for war crimes in Belgrade as a witness. Of course I learned many facts at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you familiar of a nickname or a code-name that was associated with Colonel Mitrovic, the term Cegar? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear about that. That was his code for the radio communication, he was Cegar 1, that was his call-sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were his men sometimes referred to as Cegari, if that's the right term in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to take up some of your time again. The entire unit had the call-sign Cegar and he was at the head of that unit so his call-sign was Cegar 1, and then the other officers were Cegar 2, Cegar 3, and I don't know how many there were. These were official call-signs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you about an Exhibit Number P3126. And I'm sorry, I don't have this in B/C/S. This is an English translation of an article that reportedly appeared in Tanjug on the 16th of May, 1999, and it mentions that 15 interior ministry members of the Prizren district were promoted into higher ranks, and it says Colonel Milos Vojnovic congratulated the group of decorated and promoted policemen." Do you recall that promotion ceremony on the 16th of May?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, but I don't think that there was ceremony. We were in a basement at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall who those 15 members were who got promoted -- maybe not by name, but can you tell me what units they belonged to? Were there any members of the 37th PJP Detachment or the 5th PJP Company?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were commended and received awards and they were promoted by the minister, and these were employees of the secretariat of the interior in Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Were any of them in the PJP?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably so, but I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did Mitrovic get promoted?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mitrovic is not an employee of the secretariat in Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But did he get promoted, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know, maybe he did. Maybe the minister promoted him. Before that I was in Belgrade, I mean that's where I was given this task, but I really don't know whether Mitrovic was promoted. I know that after the end of the war that he was promoted -- no, not promoted, he was commended, he was, I was, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The last document I want to ask you about is Exhibit P1188. I'll hand you a hard copy of it, and I may ask you to read some of it for me because parts of our translation have been noted as being illegible although the B/C/S copy seems to be quite legible. It's a two-sided sheet. Can you look at the one that has number 94 handwritten and circled on it. And this is a dispatch -- I think dispatch number 145 dated the 28th of May, 1999, is it to all SUPs in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but to the chiefs of the crime police departments, so it wasn't sent to the chiefs of SUPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. To the chiefs of the crime police in each of those seven secretariats, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could you read the first line because I have a question about how it's translated.

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "It is necessary that by the 29th of May, 1999, Saturday, by 1500 hours at the latest you come to the MUP staff in Pristina and to bring for the period between the 4th of March and the 23rd of May information about all the crimes committed in your" --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you. Thank you. And you'll see further down that one of the bits of information it asks for is the total number of dead bodies found and how they were registered. Do you see that in the last paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on the back side of that document you'll see what appears to be a dispatch of the same day to the same people and it's described as correction to dispatch number 145. And in the last paragraph my translation says: "Information on the number of unknown bodies found." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, what does it say? Are you on the side with the -- not the 84 --

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking at the page where it says 84. "Information about the total number of NN bodies found," and on the other side it says: "Information on the total number of bodies or corpses found."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And does not NN mean unknown?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's hard for me to interpret this now. It is possible that the author meant the corpses who had been unidentified, and perhaps he also meant crimes that involved NN perpetrators. To be precise, I'm referring to NN corpses, that is to say unidentified ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vojnovic, then the last thing I wanted to ask you about, you mentioned that -- you told us that you sometimes by nature I'm such that I unintentionally forget things, figures, names, and so on. How long has that been a problem for you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a very good memory for things I'm interested in and when it's fresh in my memory and when I acquainted myself with it in detail. Of course I'm the kind of person that I -- that does make, I mean, well, a selection. So of course it's harder for me to remember things I don't know enough about, and then these names and years and what have you not. I usually remember either the last name or the first name or nothing. I came across quite a few people and I usually expected them to know me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I do have a short one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're getting close to the end. I would like to ask you the following: When you used members of the OPG, were they OPG at that moment or were they regular policemen at the Prizren SUP?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regular policemen at the Prizren SUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just give me a moment on that, Mr. Lukic. I don't know at the moment if this is important or not, but the impression that was created earlier by your evidence was that the OPG might be used for regular activities where there was a measure of complexity, a difficult arrest or whatever. Is this distinction between them working as OPG and working as regular policemen not a rather artificial one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, but I did not quite understand this word that was used, "umjetno," but they were called OPG, operative pursuit groups; but when I led them they were regular policemen of the Prizren SUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You gave the impression yesterday that -- and indeed today that the men you had who were trained in the OPG would be used for complex arrests, for example, which suggests that they were picked out from the regular policemen for that job. Now, is that a wrong impression for us to form?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So in other words, they were used by you because of their specialist training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's just try to explain this a bit further. Members of the OPG, were they actually members of the PJP company of Prizren?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How was it that they became PJP or OPG?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were regular policemen from the secretariat in Prizren with some additional training. When a PJP unit is mobilised, then they would become members of that company of the special police unit in Prizren. When I would use them on a particular assignment, say bringing in a dangerous person, going to deal with an ambush, arresting a person and so on, then we would call them OPG.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: P1998 was shown to you yesterday. This is an analysis of the 549th Motorised Brigade. You said that a man was arrested and the report says that nine persons were killed. I would like to ask you the following. Can you give us any details about the arrested person?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to be more specific, what details?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is the action in Jeskovo in the report says that there were nine persons killed?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean how this arrest took place?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It just so happens that I do remember that particular case because during the course of the night after these activities were over, that person left that village in the direction of the town of Prizren and he came across a police patrol that was somewhere near the entrance into town. He was wearing a track suit and he was suspicious because he, or rather, he was a suspect because he had no documents on him, so they brought him in and also he had a cordless phone on him, not a mobile phone, a cordless phone. And then the next day their officers told me that during this activity and during the night he was on a tree, so that's probably why I remember. So that person was prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During his interviews while he was processed from an operative point of view, was it established that he had taken part on the KLA side in Jeskovo?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, such a leading question again in re-examination produces a valueless answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll try to avoid it in future. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is the police duty-bound to inform the army when they arrest someone, as was the case in this particular case?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a citizen, a civilian. We, I mean the members of the police, are only duty-bound to provide information to the army when it is a military person, a soldier, who is in question, in this case we didn't inform anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it possible then that the army are talking about somebody else when they say nine were killed and one was arrested?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, the report from General Delic says nine were killed, no one was arrested, no one was captured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ah, I'm sorry. Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to move on faster, I don't really want to spend more time on this, in relation to this there are KVM reports, 5D112, 5D113, and 5D114 respectively where there is a reference to nine persons who had been killed were wearing black uniforms and that the KLA had emptied Jeskovo even before the fighting took place. Members of the 5th Company of the Prizren PJP, who are they responsible to from the point of view of discipline?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Prizren secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To who are they responsible from a disciplinary point of view, I mean the members of the 37th Detachment of the PJP?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To their own original secretariats.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please call up in e-court 6D365.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My colleague Mr. Hannis asked you about this document and he asked you about disciplinary responsibility of those policemen who were charged with taking money from Albanians in order to get them out of Kosovo, and what was said to you was that we cannot see whether a criminal report was filed in this case. Do you see the document in front of you, I mean on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have it in front of me and of course you can see that a criminal report had been filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please, just tell me what's on the first page.

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we just see the name that is referred to here on this first page, who is this in this criminal report?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vukajlo Vulic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then if you look further down, in the English version it's page 2. Could you please tell us what is the crime concerned, what is the qualification? It's at the very bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For reasonable suspicion that crime was committed of settling for disproportional profit from Article 182, paragraph 1 of the Republic of Serbia Criminal Code.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us please look at the last page in Serbian and the one-but-last page in English, this same document. Could it please be zoomed in. Could you please read out the second paragraph which says: "On the basis of the statement ..." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, now I see it, yes. "On the basis of the statements made by persons of Albanian ethnic background, it can be concluded that policemen Nebojsa Lalic and Zoran Radovic and civilian persons Veselin Cimbaljevic and Vukajlo Vulic were supposed to receive as a reward 10.100 Deutschemarks for transferring two Albanian -- the two Albanian families, that they would -- and they would split the amount equally."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So is this a crime committed or was it an attempt, they were supposed to get?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had not been completed, so it was an attempt.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, remind me, who were the criminal proceedings against?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Against -- I think the first page is this Vulic Vukajlo, who is the last mentioned of these four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And also Radovic, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the subsequent pages we can find all these names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, but you looked at page 1 and 2 -- let me see it. I need to go back and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't have that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Vulic is a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, two police officers and two civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, we have Vulic on page 1. If you go on to the English page 2, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may assist, Lalic is mentioned on page 3 of the English. The second civilian is on page 4 of the English, and the second policeman, Radovic, is named on page 6 of the English. This is the criminal report, not criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed. It purports, though, to relate to all four.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] P1966, could it please be displayed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know if that's the correct number, it's listed as 1966 in the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 1996, probably I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is minutes of the meeting held in the MUP staff, and we need page 9 in Serbian and page 11 in the English. [In English] I can't find the reference now. I'll ask the witness without the document. I can't find it right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember that at one point you were shown a document where it was stated that Obrad Stevanovic had said ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, now I see it. Could we please have P1996 on the screens again, page 9. We need the third paragraph from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You see what it says here: "In the organization of the secretariat of the Ministry of the Interior in Kosovo and Metohija there clearly has to be organization that would ensure that all detachments of the PJPs must be subordinated to the chief of the secretariat." Let me ask you, is there a single police regulation that says "subordinated"?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm pretty familiar with all police regulations and there is no such term used.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you were asked whether these detachments were subordinated to you, and you explained how they were used. Tell us, what is your understanding of this? What is your understanding of what this police general says? What was it that he was trying to say by using this military term? Do you understand him at all?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did he want to say?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wanted to say that I, in a military sense, command these units; or in a police sense, I lead these units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you lead these units and did you lead the detachments of the PJP that were in your territory?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. This kind of leading, control, is a far broader concept. I could not replace the commander, I could not dismiss him, I could not punish him, I could not send him here or there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What were your powers then in relation to members of the PJP detachment that was sent to your territory, tell us so that we can understand what it was that you could do.

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I provided logistics for them, we discussed regular tasks by way of agreement, and I've already said that when the members of this detachment were carrying out their regular tasks and work it was their own officer in charge who was in charge of them. I provided accommodation, fuel, health services, vehicle repairs, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Within this regular work, did they do anything in the territory of your SUP?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they did. They patrolled and they were on the beat. This was the basic activity, the basic form of activity, or rather, police organization of work. They also worked at check-points, they held the territory, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 20, line 16, you tried to say what the refugees were telling you because you had personal contact with them. What were the people who were leaving telling you? Why was it that they were leaving?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several times I went out to these columns and talked to the people there. For the most part what was said was that they were afraid of bombing, that practically they had been ordered by their political leaders and that members of terrorist gangs were expelling them; and to tell you the truth, there were some people who did not know what to say to me, they didn't know why they were leaving, they were leaving and they themselves did not know why. I personally talked to these people several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have a call-sign? We heard of -- about Mitrovic, of his call-sign of Cegar. Did you have a call-sign?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sara 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers. We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Just one further matter, Mr. Vojnovic. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You were asked just now about PJP detachment, and the example is the 37th Detachment, carrying out regular duties such as patrolling or manning check-points which are your responsibility as -- and the responsibility of your subordinates. If you decided on duties for members of the PJP of that nature and they failed to do as they were told, who would have authority to deal with them?

utterances.speaker: MILOS VOJNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The secretariat from which the policemen had been sent from; however, I would have to draw an official note on the conduct of that particular member of the force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Anything arise from that for you, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Nothing from that, Your Honour. I just have to inform you officially that redacted version is uploaded of the statement of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall allow it to replace the original. Mr. Vojnovic, thank you. That completes your evidence. You may now leave the courtroom with the usher. Thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good-bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we shall now adjourn and resume at ten past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, our next witness is Mr. Branislav Debeljkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And we just intend to introduce his statement and we don't have any direct for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Debeljkovic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll now be examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Debeljkovic.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DEBELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have your statement before you, the one you signed?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DEBELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I will take it out. I do have the statement now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is this the statement you gave to Mr. Sreten Lukic's Defence team?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DEBELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you were to testify today, would you still repeat what you had said in the statement?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DEBELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we wish to tender Mr. Debeljkovic's statement. The number should be 6D1533.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Any cross-examination by Defence counsel? No. Mr. Debeljkovic, you'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Ms. Kravetz. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Debeljkovic.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DEBELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I have very few questions for you today, so I think we'll be done with your testimony soon. I want to begin by asking you some questions about your statement. In paragraph 17 of your statement you speak about the reporting of your activities as head of the crime police department, and you tell us that you sent reports on all incidents, measures, and actions that your department took to the crime police administration in Belgrade, the operations centre, and also to the MUP staff in Pristina. And I would like to ask you, with what frequency were these reports about your activities and on the incidents that took place in your municipality sent to the MUP staff in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DEBELJKOVIC
utterances.text: The crime police administration in Belgrade at the MUP seat was my superior administration. The chief of the administration was my superior.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DEBELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Concerning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Debeljkovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- stop you there. It's a very simple question. You say you sent reports on incidents that took place in your municipality to the MUP staff in Pristina. And I just to know how regularly did you send these reports, was it every month, every week, every day, with which frequency did this happen?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DEBELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Before answering, I have to say that when it comes to reporting there was urgent reporting that was in existence as well as periodical reporting concerning all events and occurrences, including crimes committed in the territory of the SUP that I worked for, I informed the crime police administration of those as well as the MUP staff in Pristina so that they would be informed of those events. It happened frequently. However, on occasion I did not inform the MUP staff in Pristina, but as for the crime police administration at the seat of the MUP, they were always informed of those matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say that these were regular reports that you sent on incidents that took place, criminal incidents that took place in your municipality? I'm talking specifically about the MUP staff.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DEBELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Regular as well as periodical, both to the MUP staff and administration. As for any regular reporting that was sent to the staff, I don't remember that we were under any obligation to inform the staff regularly. My obligation was to inform the crime police administration in Belgrade, to inform them regularly, and then simultaneously we would send a report to the staff; but it was simply because of the fact that I had to send it to the administration in Belgrade and then the MUP staff would be notified as well so that the staff as a body --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Debeljkovic, we should say to you, that doesn't really make much sense to us, you ought to know this. Reporting is a formality and we've evidence in this case of reports being made to the MUP staff in Pristina simultaneously with going to the headquarters. Now, the impression you've left in my mind at the moment is that it was up to you, you could decide to send it to the MUP staff or you could decide not to bother; is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand your question. It wasn't dependent on me alone. There were certain occasions in which I would receive an instructional dispatch from my administration concerning a security issue. It often happened that such a dispatch would not reach the MUP staff, it went directly to the SUP where I worked, or rather, to the crime prevention department. After taking measures, I would reply. The reply would be sent to the administration in Belgrade and sometimes the MUP staff in Pristina would not be informed of that. It wasn't a rule per se, but I just wanted to mention it. The staff was not in direct line of communication between myself and the crime police administration in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why bother reporting to them at all then? We're trying to understand when you would actually report to them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The questions right from the beginning of your cross-examination have been about the MUP staff, not about anything else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dispatches went simultaneously to the police administration and the MUP staff in Pristina concerning all crimes committed in the territory of the secretariat as well as concerning other security-related matters. The principal addressee was the crime police administration in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not finished on this, but it's back to you, Ms. Kravetz, and we'll see how you get on -- no, no, no, let's see how you get on with it with it; and if necessary, we shall return to the subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you spoke about dispatches being sent to the SUP. Your SUP chief, the SUP chief of Urosevac municipality, was required to report to the MUP staff on a daily basis; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DEBELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. It was within his sphere of activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, you tell us in your statement that you worked as the head of the crime police department in Urosevac municipality, the SUP, for ten years; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DEBELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I spent my entire career at the Urosevac SUP; from 1995 onwards I was the chief of the crime police department, but, yes, one could say that the period was about a decade at that post. Before that my posts were of a lower rank.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So you were with the MUP for, say, I suppose at least 20 years; would that be correct, a MUP employee?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DEBELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you're saying that despite the fact that you spent so many years in the MUP staff -- in the MUP and particularly at the SUP in Urosevac, you're not familiar with the reporting procedures of the SUP and of the SUP chief in particular?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DEBELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I am familiar with the reporting procedures of the SUP chief when I was supposed to inform him, but as to what he was doing on his part I am not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So after having spent 20 years working at the SUP in Urosevac, you're telling us you have no idea what were the tasks of the SUP chief and what were his obligations toward his superiors; is that what you're saying really?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DEBELJKOVIC
utterances.text: You asked me whether the SUP chief was duty-bound to daily report to the staff on certain events. Again, I can say that I don't know whether the chief of SUP was under any obligation to do that regularly, to inform the staff daily concerning certain events.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were any reports sent by the SUP chief to the MUP staff, I'm not only talking about daily reports. Just did you ever while you were there at the SUP did you ever see any reports being prepared and signed by your -- by the SUP chief addressed to the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DEBELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Never? Bozidar Filic was the chief of the SUP in Urosevac during the period you worked there, correct, in -- from April -- mid-April 1999 onwards?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DEBELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: He recently testified before this court and told the court that he was, or at least that's how he understood it, required to report daily to the MUP staff. Are you contradicting his evidence here in court?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DEBELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to tell you the following. When we were in the MUP building before the air-strikes, the chief of SUP had his office, his duties, his tasks --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir I'm going to stop you there. I'm asking a very, very precise question. I'm telling you we just had your former chief testify here, who told us that he had this duty to report regularly to the MUP staff and I'm just asking you whether you accept his testimony as being true and correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think the gentleman said "I don't know." Now he was asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me deal with this. I think the way that this question ought to be put, Ms. Kravetz, is to ask the witness whether he has any basis for contradicting that evidence. It's not for him to tell us whether to accept it or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, do you have any basis for contradicting the testimony that Mr. Filic gave just some days ago here in this court?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DEBELJKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot either confirm or deny that part of his testimony. First of all, we were physically separated, we were not in the building of our SUP, we were in different locations for security reasons because of the bombardment. He was in one part of the town and my service was in another, and then another service was in the third part of the town and so on and so forth. As of the 15th of April we seldom met. Even had we been in the same building of the SUP, I really could not have known what the chief of the SUP was doing. My scope of activity was crime, prevention of crime, and that's what I was dealing with. A great many people that I headed worked on that, and the issues we worked on were voluminous, time-consuming. I had no time to worry about who or what the chief of the SUP was informing and reporting. I don't know if you catch my drift, but that's the truth, the only truth I can tell you. I cannot speculate or assume, I can neither confirm nor deny.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Very well, sir. You tell us in your statement - and this is at paragraph 29 - that in 1998 you went several times to the MUP staff, delivered general information about crimes. What was the purpose of you handing over this information to the MUP staff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you said 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, it is 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: It's in his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I went to the building where, among other things, the staff was located. I remember I took there certain documents with crime statistics, probably so that the staff could monitor what the situation was with crime. It was not of any interest of mine what they were doing with that further. Often with the assistant head of the staff, I had telephone conversations. Sometimes he would call me, on other occasions I would call him. He wanted to know what the situation in the field was, how we were doing, what the statistics were of crimes and unidentified perpetrators, et cetera. He wanted to know if there was prevalence of any particular type of crime in which they could assist professionally if needed. We also discussed technical issues. Usually it would take place during the morning. It wasn't daily, it wasn't an obligation of mine to give him a call every morning I come into the office, but frequently I talked to the assistant in charge of crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And who was that at the time?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DEBELJKOVIC
utterances.text: During the war it was Tomislav Blagojevic; before him, it was Novica Zdravkovic. I spoke to him more. The pattern of communication I described was with the -- with him. Even before him there was a Simic. I also frequently spoke with him. He would also come over to the SUP building where he would spend an hour or two discussing the situation in the field and he would share information on other SUPs, say, the one of Gnjilane and how they dealt with certain problems, et cetera. This is what we would usually discuss. I would also report to him what crimes occurred in the previous period, how many thefts, whether there was pick-pocketing, aggravated thefts, and what was particularly interesting for him to hear was to know whether there were any crimes involving use of fire-arms, more serious offences. We simply exchanged information. I believe people were elected to the staff for their professionalism and experience, and they could provide data and instruction to work more efficiently in preventing crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Debeljkovic, can you think of any particular benefit that you derived from the MUP staff by providing this information or because other SUPs provided it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it comes to professional assistance, I cannot recall a situation in which the assistant in charge of crime assisted me particularly or significantly helping me to shed light on a certain crime, but the exchange of opinions must have been useful for work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You spoke about Tomislav Blagojevic and you said before him the person you spoke to was Novica Zdravkovic. Do you know what was the --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DEBELJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- position that these gentlemen had at the MUP staff? What position did they occupy?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DEBELJKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were assistant heads of the staff in crime prevention. This is what I can recall off the cuff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you told us you had these contacts -- I mean, you went there in 1998. Did you or anyone from your department continue to provide -- have this sort of contact and provide this sort of information to the MUP staff in 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV DEBELJKOVIC
utterances.text: As the issues were growing in complexity and as there was an increase in terrorist activities, our contacts ... well, I didn't go to the staff itself, especially once the air-strikes began I saw no staff member. I wasn't visited by any of them and I didn't go to Pristina to take any information there or for any other reason. Our communication with the staff was made very difficult because the telephone lines were cut off and it was dangerous to use the roads to Pristina. All those things resulted in our contacts becoming more and more infrequent. I even recall a situation at the beginning of the bombardment --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
